reqF: Shorten a long URL to a 7-character code
Redirect a code to the original URL
Optional custom alias and expiry
Click counts per link
reqN: Redirect p99 under 50 ms
Very read heavy: 100 reads per write
Highly available: a dead link is a broken promise
Codes must never collide
est: Writes: 100M/day ≈ 1,200/s, peaks ~5k/s
Reads: 100x ≈ 120k/s, peaks ~500k/s
Storage: 100M x 500 B x 365 x 5 yr ≈ 90 TB
Cache: top 20% of daily reads ≈ a few hundred GB
data: urls: code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at
Key-value store partitioned by code
clicks: append-only events to Kafka, rolled up in the warehouse

blocks.u: Start from the people clicking links: almost all traffic is redirects.
blocks.lb: Spreads redirect traffic across stateless API servers.
blocks.api: Stateless service: creates codes and serves redirects.
blocks.id: Hands out unique 64-bit ids; base62 of the id is the code, so no collisions.
blocks.c: Hot codes live in Redis: most redirects never touch the DB.
blocks.db: Key-value store, partitioned by code: one lookup per miss.
blocks.k: Click events go to a queue so redirects stay fast.
blocks.w: Analytics runs offline on the warehouse, not on the hot path.

dives: How do you generate codes without collisions?
A Snowflake-style id generator, then base62. 7 chars = 3.5 trillion codes. No check-and-retry needed.
301 is cached by browsers (fewer hits, no click tracking). 302 every time (lets you count clicks).
How do you keep redirects under 50 ms?
Cache hot codes (80/20 rule), CDN or edge for the top links, KV store sharded by code.
Custom aliases?
Check-and-set insert on the alias; reject if taken.
wrap: Bottleneck: the KV store on cache misses. Fix: bigger cache, read replicas.
Abuse: rate limit creation per user, scan for malicious URLs.
Next: expiry cleanup job, analytics dashboards.

reqF: Limit requests per user, IP or API key
Different rules per endpoint
Return 429 with Retry-After when over the limit
Rules change without a deploy
reqN: Adds under 1-2 ms per request
Works across many gateway nodes
Fails open if the limiter is down
Accurate enough, not perfect
est: 1M requests/s at the edge
10M active keys x ~100 B ≈ 1 GB of counters
One Redis round trip per request: shard Redis by key
data: counters in Redis: key = rule:user:window → count, TTL
rules: id, match (path, method), limit, window, scope

blocks.u: Clients of every kind hit one front door.
blocks.gw: The limiter lives in the gateway so every service is protected.
blocks.s: Allowed requests pass straight to the services.
blocks.r: Shared counters in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script.
blocks.cfg: Rules come from config, so limits change without a deploy.
blocks.x: Over the limit: 429 plus Retry-After, so clients back off.

dives: Which algorithm?
Token bucket: allows short bursts, simple, most common. Sliding window counter if you need smoother limits.
How do you stay correct across many gateways?
Central Redis with an atomic Lua script (INCR + check + EXPIRE in one step).
What if Redis is down?
Fail open with a local in-memory fallback limit, and alert.
Hot keys?
Shard counters by key; keep a local token cache for very hot clients.
wrap: Bottleneck: Redis round trip. Fix: local batching, shard by key.
Next: per-plan limits, dashboards of who is throttled.

reqF: 1:1 and group chat
Online presence and last seen
Sent, delivered and read receipts
Messages reach offline users later
Photos and files
reqN: Delivery under 200 ms when both are online
Messages never lost, kept in order per chat
Billions of messages a day
Works on flaky mobile networks
est: 500M DAU x 40 msgs ≈ 20B msgs/day ≈ 230k/s
Storage: 20B x 100 B ≈ 2 TB/day
Open connections: ~100M at peak, ~50k per server ≈ 2k servers
data: messages: chat_id (partition), msg_id (sort), sender, body, ts
chats + members tables
presence in Redis with TTL heartbeats

blocks.a: User A on a phone with a long-lived connection.
blocks.b: User B, maybe on another server or offline.
blocks.w1: WebSocket servers keep open connections for 2-way realtime.
blocks.w2: Each user is pinned to one chat server.
blocks.k: The queue routes messages between servers and absorbs bursts.
blocks.p: Presence lives in Redis with heartbeats and TTLs.
blocks.db: Cassandra: partition by chat, sort by message id, fast writes.
blocks.push: Offline users get a push, then sync when they reconnect.
blocks.s3: Media goes to object storage and a CDN, not through chat servers.

dives: How do you keep order?
Per-chat sequence ids assigned on write; clients sort by them.
How do you avoid duplicates?
Client message id = idempotency key; server dedupes.
Group chat with 500 members?
Fan out through the queue; big groups use pull on open.
How do you know who is online?
Heartbeats every ~30 s into Redis with a TTL.
wrap: Bottleneck: connection servers. Fix: scale horizontally, a registry of user → server.
Next: end-to-end encryption, message search.

reqF: Post text, photos and links
See a feed of people you follow, newest or ranked
Like and comment
Infinite scroll
reqN: Feed loads in under 200 ms
300M DAU, heavy reads
A new post can take a few seconds to appear
Celebrities with 100M followers
est: Reads: 300M x 10 feed loads ≈ 35k/s
Writes: 300M x 0.5 posts ≈ 1.7k/s
Fan-out: avg 200 followers ≈ 350k feed inserts/s
data: posts: post_id, author_id, body, media, created_at
follows: follower_id, followee_id
feed cache: user_id → list of post ids

blocks.u: Readers open the feed far more than they post.
blocks.gw: Auth and routing for posts and feed reads.
blocks.k: New-post events decouple writing from fan-out.
blocks.fo: Workers push the post id into each follower's feed.
blocks.g: Who follows whom, read by the fan-out workers.
blocks.fc: Each feed is a Redis list of post ids, ready to read.
blocks.cdn: Images and video come from the CDN.

dives: Fan-out on write or read?
Write for most users (fast reads). Read-time pull for celebrities. Merge both: hybrid.
Why store ids, not posts, in the feed?
Small lists; hydrate post details from cache at read time.
Pagination?
Cursor based (last post id), never offset.
Ranking?
A ranking service scores candidates; start with recency.
wrap: Bottleneck: fan-out for big accounts. Fix: hybrid fan-out.
Next: ranking model, ads insertion, notifications.

reqF: Upload videos
Watch with smooth playback on any device
Adapt quality to network speed
Video page: title, views, recommendations
reqN: Start playback in under 2 s
Huge egress: CDN serves almost everything
Uploads resumable
Durable: never lose a video
est: Uploads: 500 hours per minute
Each video stored in ~6 renditions ≈ 5x raw size
Egress: millions of concurrent streams x ~5 Mbps ≈ Tbps, so CDN
data: videos: id, owner, title, status, renditions
segments in object storage: /video/rendition/segment.ts

blocks.up: Hands out pre-signed URLs so uploads go straight to storage.
blocks.raw: Raw uploads land in object storage.
blocks.q: Each upload becomes a transcode job.
blocks.tr: Workers split, encode many bitrates and merge.
blocks.cdn: The CDN serves the bytes, close to viewers.
blocks.v: Viewers stream segments and switch quality on the fly.
blocks.api: Video API serves the watch page and manifest.
blocks.meta: Metadata DB: titles, status, view counts.

dives: Why pre-signed uploads?
Big files skip your servers; resumable multipart upload to S3.
Adaptive bitrate?
Client picks the next segment's quality from measured bandwidth.
How do you transcode fast?
Split into chunks, encode in parallel as a DAG, merge.
Cost of egress?
CDN with high hit ratio, pre-warm popular videos at the edge.
wrap: Bottleneck: transcode backlog. Fix: autoscale workers, prioritise popular creators.
Next: recommendations, live streaming.

reqF: Rider requests a ride
Match the nearest available driver
Live driver location and ETA
Pay at the end of the trip
reqN: Matching in a few seconds
1M drivers sending location every 4 s
A driver is never offered two trips at once
Highly available in every city
est: Location writes: 1M / 4 s = 250k/s
Ride requests: ~1k/s at peak
Location data is small and short-lived: keep it in memory
api: WS: driver location updates, ride status pushes
data: trips: id, rider, driver, status, route, fare
driver locations: in-memory geo index (H3 / geohash)

blocks.r: Riders request trips and watch the car arrive.
blocks.d: Drivers stream their location every few seconds.
blocks.t: Trip service owns the ride lifecycle.
blocks.l: Location service ingests 250k updates per second.
blocks.m: Matching finds and locks the best nearby driver.
blocks.geo: In-memory geo index for nearby search.
blocks.tdb: Trips DB: durable record of every ride.
blocks.maps: Maps and ETA service for routes and arrival times.
blocks.pay: Payment runs when the trip ends.

dives: Why not store locations in a database?
250k writes/s of data that expires in seconds: keep it in memory (Redis GEO / H3 cells).
How do you find nearby drivers?
Look up the rider's cell and its neighbours, then rank by ETA.
How do you avoid double booking a driver?
Lock the driver (atomic set with TTL) while the offer is open.
What if a region's servers fail?
Partition by city; failover per region.
wrap: Bottleneck: location ingest. Fix: shard by geo cell.
Next: surge pricing, pooled rides.

reqF: Send push, SMS and email
Respect user preferences and opt-outs
Templates per message type

reqN: 10M+ notifications a day, bursts

dives: How do you avoid duplicates?
Idempotency key per notification; workers check before sending.
What if a provider is down?
Retry with backoff, then dead-letter queue; failover to a second provider.
Quiet hours?
Delay into a scheduled queue by user time zone.
Rate limits?
Per-user caps so nobody gets spammed.
wrap: Bottleneck: provider limits. Fix: per-channel throttling, multiple providers.

reqF: Crawl the web from seed URLs
Store page content
Extract and follow links
Re-crawl pages to keep them fresh
reqN: 1B pages a month ≈ 400 pages/s

Skip duplicates
Robust to traps and bad HTML

Storage: 1B x 500 KB ≈ 500 TB/month (compress)

blocks.cs: Raw pages go to object storage.
blocks.dd: A Bloom filter drops URLs already seen.
blocks.seen: The durable set of seen URLs.

dives: How are you polite?
One queue per host, a delay between requests, obey robots.txt.
Duplicates?
URL dedupe with a Bloom filter; content dedupe with simhash.
Crawler traps?
Max depth, URL length limits, per-site page caps.
Freshness?
Re-crawl by page change rate and importance.
wrap: Bottleneck: DNS and network. Fix: DNS cache, more fetchers per region.
Next: JavaScript rendering, ranking signals.

reqF: Customer pays at checkout
Charge through a payment provider
Record every money movement
Handle refunds
reqN: Never charge twice
Never lose a payment: strong consistency
Auditable to the cent
Reconciled with the provider every day
est: 1M payments/day ≈ 12/s average, 100x peaks on sale days
Small data, high stakes: correctness over speed
data: payments: id, order_id, amount, status (state machine), idempotency_key UNIQUE
ledger_entries: account, debit, credit, payment_id (append-only)

blocks.u: The customer presses Pay.
blocks.co: Checkout creates the order and calls payments.
blocks.pdb: Payments DB holds the state machine.
blocks.wh: Webhooks confirm results from the provider.
blocks.led: Double-entry ledger: every debit has a credit.
blocks.rec: Daily reconciliation against the provider's settlement file.

dives: How do you never charge twice?
Idempotency key with a UNIQUE constraint; retries return the first result.
What states can a payment be in?
CREATED → PENDING → SUCCEEDED / FAILED, only forward.
Why a ledger?
Append-only double-entry: balances always add up and are auditable.
What if the webhook never arrives?
Poll the provider for pending payments; reconcile daily.
wrap: Bottleneck: provider latency. Fix: async confirmation via webhooks.
Next: multi-currency, payouts, chargebacks.

reqF: Show top 5 suggestions as the user types
Rank by popularity
Update with trending queries
Filter unsafe terms
reqN: Under 100 ms per keystroke
10B queries a day
Suggestions can be an hour stale
est: 10B queries x ~5 keystrokes ≈ 600k lookups/s
Unique prefixes: hundreds of millions; top-k cached per prefix fits in memory per shard

query logs → hourly counts

blocks.u: Users type a few letters.

blocks.log: Every query is logged to a stream.

dives: Why cache top-k per node?
Lookup becomes O(prefix length), no tree walk at query time.
How do you update?
Rebuild offline from logs and swap atomically.
Scale?
Shard by prefix range; replicate hot shards.
Client tricks?
Debounce typing, cache in the browser.
wrap: Bottleneck: hot prefixes like 'a'. Fix: replicate, cache at the edge.
Next: personalisation, multiple languages.

Keep file versions
Share files

Strong consistency for file metadata
Durable storage
Works offline, syncs later

data: files: id, path, owner, version, chunk_list

blocks.bs: Block service accepts only the chunks that changed.

blocks.nt: Other devices are told something changed.

dives: Why chunk files?
Upload only changed 4 MB chunks; dedupe identical chunks by hash.
Conflicts?
Version check on commit; on conflict keep both copies.
Why SQL for metadata?
Transactions for versions and paths.
How do devices find out?
Long poll or WebSocket notifications, then fetch changes.

Book and pay

reqN: Never double-book a seat

Hold with SET NX EX in Redis, plus a UNIQUE (event, seat) in the DB.
What happens if payment fails?
The hold expires or is released; the seat returns.
Flash sale?
Waiting room, cached event pages, admit in batches.
Fairness?
Queue position by arrival, block bots.

reqF: Answer a natural-language question in a few sentences
Ground the answer in fresh web pages
Show 3-6 citations the user can click
Handle follow-up questions in the same thread
reqN: First tokens in about 1-2 s, full answer in a few seconds
Citations must actually support the sentence they sit on
Fresh: news from today should be findable
Cost per answer low enough for a free tier
est: Assume 100M questions/day = ~1,200/s, peaks ~5k/s
Fan-out: 3-8 sub-queries each = ~10-40k searches/s
Retrieve ~100-1,000 candidates, rerank to 5-20 passages
Context: 10 passages x ~300 tokens = ~3k tokens per answer
data: Web index: url, title, passages, crawl_ts, language, authority signals
Inverted index (BM25) + vector index (ANN) over passages
answer log: question, sub_queries, passages_used, citations, model_version

blocks.u: Start from the user's question - it is usually vague or compound.
blocks.rw: An LLM rewrites the question and fans it out into several focused searches (query fan-out).
blocks.web: Gate 1: only pages the crawler indexed can ever be cited.
blocks.kw: BM25 keyword search - wins on exact names, numbers and rare words.
blocks.vx: Vector (ANN) search - wins on meaning and paraphrases.
blocks.fu: Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges both lists without tuning score scales.
blocks.rr: A cross-encoder reranks the top ~100 down to ~10. Gate 3: only these reach the model.
blocks.llm: The LLM writes the answer from the passages in its context window.
blocks.cite: Gate 4: the model picks which passages to cite - the only opaque gate.

dives: Why not just use vector search?
One vector per passage averages away specifics, so exact names and compound queries (X AND Y) get missed. BM25 catches literal matches; fuse both with RRF, then rerank.
Why a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank?
Cheap first stage for recall over millions of passages, expensive cross-encoder only on the top ~100 for precision. Classic cheap structure in front of an expensive operation.
How do you keep citations honest?
Cite at passage level, check each sentence is supported by its cited passage (an entailment check or an LLM judge), and drop citations that fail.
How do you measure quality?
A golden set of questions with judged passages: recall@100 for retrieval, nDCG@10 after rerank, citation precision, and human or LLM-judge answer quality - re-run on every model change.
How do you keep it fresh?
Re-crawl news and high-change pages often, a small fresh index merged at query time, and recency as a ranking feature.

Search-enabled API calls cost about $10-25 per 1,000. At 3.6M answers/day that is $36k+/day, more than ~$14k/day revenue at $5M ARR. So: share runs across tenants, adaptive sampling, weekly cadence for the long tail, batch pricing for parsing, and compare API vs browser vs data-partner cost per answer.
How do you stop retries double counting?
Idempotent job key = project + prompt + engine + region + day + run number, a unique constraint on run, and upserts into the facts table.
API answers differ from what users see in the app. What do you do?
Be explicit per engine: official API with web search on, headless browser runs from target regions for spot checks, and track the gap as its own metric.
How do you cut cost?
Dedupe identical prompt + engine + region + day across tenants, batch APIs for parsing, rules before LLM, small model for parsing, weekly cadence for long-tail prompts.
How do you parse mentions reliably?
Alias dictionary per brand (names, products, misspellings), URL -> domain -> brand for citations, a small LLM only for ambiguous cases, Zod/Pydantic schema validation, golden-set evals.
Postgres or ClickHouse?
Both: Postgres for config and transactions; ClickHouse for append-only facts with ORDER BY (project, day) and materialized rollups.

dives: Why not just show the latest answer?
Answers are random samples. One run tells you almost nothing; a rate over N runs with an interval tells you what users usually see.
Why Wilson and not mean +/- 2 standard errors?
At small N and rates near 0% or 100% the simple formula gives impossible ranges (below 0). Wilson stays inside 0-100% and is honest at small N.
How do you detect a real drop?
Compare this week's interval with last week's (or a two-proportion test), require a minimum N, and use rolling windows to smooth daily noise.
How do you control cost?
Adaptive sampling - stop early when the interval is already narrow, add runs only where the interval straddles a decision threshold.
An engine ships a new model. Now what?
Annotate the timeline, compare before/after on a fixed control prompt set, and avoid alerting customers on an engine-wide shift.

How do you make it faster and cheaper?
Let the model batch several tool calls in one turn (fan-out), cache tool results per day, and route simple steps to a small model.

Tiny memory for 'have I seen this URL?' - it can say 'maybe seen' by mistake (rarely skipping a page) but never misses one it has truly seen.
How do you re-crawl cheaply?
Conditional GETs with ETag / If-Modified-Since, sitemap lastmod, and content hashes to skip unchanged pages.

Only when the raw HTML is missing the main content - rendering costs about 10x a plain fetch.

Ranking quality depends on order and graded relevance; nDCG rewards putting the best results first and discounts lower positions.

How do you trust an LLM judge?
Label ~100 items with experts, measure the judge's agreement (true positive and true negative rates), fix the rubric until it agrees, then re-check on every judge model change.
Interleaving or A/B?
Interleaving for ranking comparisons - each user sees a mix, so it needs much less traffic; A/B for business metrics like conversion.

dives: Walk me through the latency budget.

Measure from the learner's last word to the tutor's first audio. Turn detection + final transcript ~300 ms, router ~100 ms, small-model first token ~300 ms, first TTS audio ~200 ms, network ~80 ms = about 1 s. Stream every stage, flush TTS per sentence, run the agent next to the room, and keep big models off the hot path.
The learner interrupts mid-sentence. What happens?

The SFU keeps listening while the tutor talks. Voice activity fires, the agent cancels TTS and the LLM stream, and uses word timings to cut its own message history at the last word actually played - so it never assumes the learner heard the rest.
How do you stop the model writing broken or unsafe UI?

A fixed component catalog with Zod schemas. The model calls draw/show3d/offerOptions tools; each action is validated before it reaches the canvas. Generated mini-simulations run in a sandboxed iframe with no network.
How does the tutor remember the learner without leaking data?

Two layers: per-session state in graph checkpoints, long-term facts in a store namespaced by learner id with embeddings for search by meaning. Every query is scoped by the session's identity, never by model output, and delete removes memories, checkpoints, recordings and events in one workflow.
How do you grade consistently?

Split the rubric into atomic questions (one per criterion) and answer them with a classifier that returns stable probabilities, then let a larger model write the explanation with evidence links. Test it: same answer in many wordings and repeated runs must get the same score.
Why spaced repetition, and how does the scheduler work?

Without review, people forget most of a lesson within days. FSRS models each item's stability and difficulty from past reviews and sets the next due date for a target recall; the Coach agent turns due items into a short nudge.
What autonomy does each agent get?

Read, Draft, Act. Reading the learner's own data and drawing on their canvas = Act. Publishing a lesson, emailing someone, sharing a report = Draft, waits for a person. Background agents may only Read or Draft. Identity always comes from the session.
How do you know a prompt change made it better, not worse?

Eval cases per behaviour (routing accuracy, option-pick accuracy, grading agreement, refusal cases) run in CI and block a drop; sampled live sessions get online evaluators; disagreements go to a human review queue that feeds new cases back in.
wrap: Bottleneck: the voice hot path - keep it on small models, colocate agent and room, measure p95 per stage.
Risk: confident wrong explanations - cite sources, check claims, and make grading auditable with evidence.
Cost: speech and big-model calls dominate - route most turns to small models and cache the system prompt.
Next: kids mode behind a policy profile, uploads (search over the learner's own notes), an MCP server for learner progress.

reqF: Employee asks in chat, the ticket tracker or Slack and gets a cited answer from the company's tools
Agent can draft and act (create a ticket, update a page) with a person's OK
Agents start on events too: a new hire, a Sev-1 incident, a deal moving stage
Connect 3rd-party tools (Drive, Slack, GitHub, Salesforce) alongside the company's own
Admins see every action an agent took and can switch agents off
reqN: Never show anything the asker can't open in the source tool - fail closed
Search answers in about a second; full RAG answers stream within a few seconds
Tenant isolation: one customer's data and caches never reach another
Predictable cost per tenant: quotas and credits, small models where they are enough
Measured quality: online success rate plus offline evals before every change
est: Assume a 10k-employee tenant: ~50M objects (pages, tickets, messages) and ~5 queries per person per day = ~50k queries/day, peak ~5/s
Index: 50M objects x ~3 chunks x 768-dim vectors (~3 KB) = ~450 GB of vectors per large tenant - shard by tenant
ACLs ride with each object: some platforms cap principals per object (around 500), so model groups, not long user lists
Only natural-language questions need full RAG; person, team and bookmark lookups return near-instantly - most traffic never touches the big model
Event-triggered agents can burst (a reorg creates 1,000 tickets): queue and throttle per tenant, never fire 1,000 LLM calls at once
api: PUT /connectors/:id/objects (bulk push objects, users, groups, relationships + permissions)
data: objects: id (ARI-style), type, tenant, properties, permissions [ACLs: AND of access controls, OR of principals]
relationships: object -> object (page <-> ticket, PR <-> service owner)

blocks.u: Start from the employee: they ask where they already work - chat, a ticket, Slack - and expect a cited answer.
blocks.trig: Agents also start on events (new hire, Sev-1, deal stage). Same agent, different entry, so the design must handle bursts.
blocks.ag: The agent plans the steps, retrieves context, and calls skills. Writes go through approval; reads don't.
blocks.rt: Small, fast classifiers pick the intent (person, team, bookmark or a real question) and rewrite the query. Big models stay off this hop.
blocks.srch: Hybrid retrieval: keyword (BM25) plus vectors, with the asker's permissions applied as a filter right inside the query.
blocks.rr: A cross-encoder reranks the top results for real relevance; popularity and freshness signals help.
blocks.perm: Before anything reaches the model, re-check each result against the source tool. Stale ACLs or a failed check = drop it.
blocks.kg: A work graph: every object carries its type, its relationships and its permissions. Agents can follow links: ticket -> page -> PR -> owner.
blocks.con: Connectors bring 3rd-party tools in three ways: full sync, light sync, or federated live search. Each pushes ACLs with the data.
blocks.gw: An AI gateway in front of every model: tenant quotas, routing, fallbacks and cost metering in one place.
blocks.llm: Model per stage: small models for routing and rewriting, a strong model for the final answer, which must decline when the context can't answer.
blocks.appr: Read tools run freely. Draft and Act tools show the plan or the change and wait for a person.
blocks.tools: Skills are typed tools tagged Read, Draft or Act - the tag decides the approval path and the audit trail.
blocks.obs: Every action is logged for admins; traces feed evals: an online success rate plus offline judge suites.

dives: How do you guarantee nobody sees a page they can't open?

Permissions travel with the data: each object stores its ACLs (AND of access controls, OR of principals). Filter at retrieval time inside the index, then re-check the final results against the source tool before the model sees them. If a user isn't mapped to an identity, or a check fails, drop the item - fail closed.
Why not one big model for every step?

Each stage has its own job. Small models matched big ones on query rewriting with lower latency; binary classifiers route to the right source; the strong model only writes the final answer and must say 'I don't know' when context is missing. Pick per stage on quality, latency and cost with its own eval set.
How do you measure if it's any good?

Online: query success rate from clicks, dwell time and thumbs. Offline: Recall@k, NDCG and MRR for retrieval, plus an LLM judge checked against human labels for answers. Freeze earlier stages when testing one stage so you know what changed.
An automation fires the agent 1,000 times and calls start failing. What now?
Tenant-level caps return 429s. Queue and stagger runs, batch where possible, back off with jitter, and log the rate limit clearly in the audit trail so admins can see why a run failed.
What can an agent do without a person?

Tag every tool Read, Draft or Act. Read runs freely. Draft produces a proposal; Act changes systems and needs approval, or a scoped standing rule. Agents started by automations only get read tools by default.
How do you plug in a customer's own system?
Build a connector: extract, map to shared object types, then bulk push objects, users, groups, relationships and permissions. Test retrieval offline with synthetic questions before real users arrive.
How do you ship this into a big customer in 12 weeks?

Discover (pick one workflow with a baseline metric), Build (connector + agent + evals), Adopt (champions, training, feedback loop), Value (report the metric against the baseline). Leave behind a pattern the next team can reuse.
wrap: Recap: hybrid retrieval with permissions checked twice, model per stage, typed tools with approvals, audit + evals.
Next: tenant-tuned embeddings, more event-triggered agents, connector kit for customers' own systems.
Risks: stale ACLs, rate-limit bursts, over-eager write actions - each has a guard above.

reqF: Teams ship their own agents (instructions, skills, tools) without building infrastructure
Users reach agents where they work: Slack DMs, shared channels, or a plain HTTP channel
Agents act on a user's behalf (their CRM, their mail) or as a service account, depending on where they were called
Long runs survive crashes, wait for a person (approval or sign-in) for days, then carry on
Agents remember user preferences and learn better procedures over time
Agents can set their own schedules ("every Monday 9:00, send my pipeline report")
reqN: Multi-tenant: no data, memory or credentials leak across users, channels or teams
Durable: a crash or deploy never loses a run; resume from the last step
Fair: a burst from one team can't starve others (priorities, limits per tenant)
Safe: generated code runs only in a sandbox; risky actions need approval
Measured: every change to prompts, skills or models passes evals first

A deep-agent run = tens of model calls and tool calls over minutes; at peak that's ~5 x 300 s = ~1,500 runs in flight -> queue + many workers, not one request thread each
Checkpoint after every step: ~30 steps x ~20 KB state = ~600 KB per run; 100k runs/day = ~60 GB/day -> keep recent checkpoints hot, expire old ones

api: POST /channels/:kind/events (Slack, GitHub, HTTP webhooks -> auth handler)
PUT /agents/:id/context (instructions, skills - versioned in the context hub)
data: threads + runs (status, priority, principal, channel)
checkpoints per thread (state after each step: resume, rewind, human in the loop)
memory store namespaces: (agent) procedures, (agent, user) preferences

blocks.ch: Start where people work: Slack DMs and channels, or an HTTP channel for any custom surface (webhooks, GitHub, your app).
blocks.auth: A central auth handler decides who is calling (a user or the agent itself) and puts that principal into the run's context.
blocks.q: Runs go on a queue served by workers (Agent Server: workers x 10 jobs each), so bursts wait their turn and long runs don't hold a web request open.
blocks.sched: Schedules are timed runs on the same queue (cron files), and the agent can create its own through a custom tool ("every Monday 9:00").
blocks.rt: The harness runs the agent loop on a durable runtime: it checkpoints every step, so it can pause, crash, resume, or wait days for a person.
blocks.hub: Instructions and skills live in a versioned context hub, so business experts edit them and promote good skills to the workspace.
blocks.gw: One LLM gateway for every model call: quotas per team, fallbacks, cost and governance in one place.
blocks.obs: Every run is traced; evals run agents in real environments with verifiers, and changes must climb the score before shipping.
blocks.mem: Memory is split by scope: what the agent learns for everyone (procedures) and what it knows about one user (preferences).
blocks.sbx: Generated code only runs inside a sandbox with no access to secrets or the network it doesn't need.
blocks.cred: Tool calls go through a credential broker: user-scoped tokens in a DM, agent-scoped service accounts in shared places. If a user hasn't signed in yet, the run pauses until they do.
blocks.mcp: Tools are mostly MCP servers (CRM, mail, search); the broker hands each call the right scoped token.

dives: What is an agent harness and why not just call the model in a loop?

Agent = model + harness. The harness is everything around the model that gets it the right context at the right time: instructions, skills loaded on demand, a filesystem to write notes and offload big outputs, a sandbox to run code, sub-agents with their own context windows, memory, and human-in-the-loop steering. A bare ReAct loop works for demos; long tasks fail without context management.
How do you manage the context window on long tasks?

Four moves: offload (tool results over ~20k tokens go to files with a short preview), compact (Deep Agents summarises at 85% of the input limit, keeps the newest 10%, saves the full history to disk), select (skills show only name + description until needed), isolate (sub-agents return only their final result).
How does the agent act on my behalf without leaking my access?

The auth handler sets the principal for each run. The credential broker picks the token from that principal and channel: my own OAuth token in a DM, a service account in a shared channel. Tokens never enter the prompt; tools get them at call time. Memory follows the same scopes, so a shared channel never sees my private memories.
The agent needs me to sign in to the CRM halfway through. What happens?

The tool asks for a user connection; none exists, so the runtime raises one interrupt (credential_authorization_required) with a sign-in link sent only to me. The run is a checkpoint, so nothing waits. When I authorise - even days later - it resumes and re-runs that step from its start.
Why a task queue instead of running the agent in the request?

Agent runs last minutes, not milliseconds. A queue gives priorities, retries, fairness and back-pressure; concurrency = workers x jobs per worker (10 by default in Agent Server). Pick a double-texting strategy for a second message mid-run: reject, enqueue (default), interrupt or rollback.
How do business experts improve the agent without engineers?
Their knowledge goes into instructions and skills in a versioned context hub. They edit, review and promote skills; every version runs the eval suite before it reaches users.
How do you evaluate an agent, not just one answer?

Run the agent in a real environment on a task, then a verifier checks the end state - Harbor tasks have an instruction, a Docker environment, tests and a reward score. Keep a dataset of real tasks, hill-climb, gate releases, and feed production traces back in.
How would you build one internal agent fast for a team for a customer team?

Start from the base harness, codify the team's expertise as skills with them, wire 2-3 tools with scoped credentials, ship to their Slack, and set up evals on their real tasks from day one. Measure one business metric against a baseline.
wrap: Recap: business logic (yours) + harness (context engineering) + infrastructure (auth, queue, durability, sandbox, gateway, evals).
Next: agent-created schedules, custom HTTP channels, per-run config for dynamic agents, A2A between agents.
Risks: credential leaks across channels, runaway cost, context rot on long runs, unsafe code - each has a guard above.

Participants join from a link, QR code, panel or message and answer by video or voice, any time of day

Peak: a panel wave of 2,000 people in 2 hours ~ 300-500 interviews live at once for one study

participants, sessions (state, current question, resume token), answers (media key, transcript id)

blocks.res: Start from the researcher: a goal and a brief in, a cited report out. They never write prompts.
blocks.app: The study builder turns a brief into a draft guide, screener and quotas; the researcher accepts or edits each suggestion.
blocks.pg: Postgres holds the system of record: tenants, studies, guide versions, sessions, quotas. Tenant id on every row.
blocks.part: Participants come from links, QR codes, panels or messages, on a phone or laptop. No app install needed.
blocks.rtc: The interview client records each answer (camera, mic, screen) and uploads it in chunks, so weak mobile data still works.
blocks.mod: The AI moderator runs one session: code walks the guide, the model phrases questions and decides when to probe.
blocks.llm: Model per job: a small, fast model for probe decisions, a stronger one for phrasing and analysis. A second provider as fallback.
blocks.s3: Recordings land in object storage under a per-tenant, per-region prefix. Raw media is kept so analysis can be re-run.
blocks.q: One queue per stage (transcode, transcribe, code, report). Jobs keyed by answer + stage, so a retry never doubles work.
blocks.mp: The media pipeline transcodes for playback and transcribes with word timestamps - the timestamps make every quote a clip.
blocks.syn: Synthesis codes each answer, clusters codes into themes across interviews and keeps a link from every theme to its quotes.
blocks.ev: Evals check the moderator and the coder before any prompt or model change ships; quote checks reject anything not in the transcript.
blocks.kb: The knowledge base indexes themes, quotes and transcripts of every study, filtered by tenant and permissions.
blocks.rep: Reports and 'ask' answers cite real quotes; click any number to hear the people behind it.

dives: Why split the live path from the analysis path?

They have different needs. The live moderator needs low latency and one session's state; analysis needs throughput, retries and the ability to re-run. Separate services, a queue between them, and the live path never waits on analysis.
How do you guarantee no invented quotes?

The coder must return a quote span (start, end) inside the transcript, not free text. A verifier checks the span is a real substring; anything that fails is dropped. Every theme stores answer id + span + media timestamp, so the UI plays the exact clip.
A panel sends 2,000 people in an hour. What protects you?

Stateless moderator workers that autoscale on live sessions, a quota engine that reserves a slot when an interview starts (and frees it on timeout), per-tenant rate limits on model calls, and queues that absorb the analysis burst.
How do quotas stay right when many people join at once?

Quota counters in Postgres updated in the same transaction as the session (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a conditional UPDATE). Reserve on start, confirm on complete, release on abandon after an idle timeout.
How do you change a prompt without breaking old studies?

Version prompts and models per stage and store the version on every result. Run the new version on a golden set first; re-run a study only when the researcher asks, and keep theme ids stable so links survive.
What does multi-tenancy look like end to end?

Tenant id on every row with row-level security, a tenant + region prefix on media, search filtered by tenant inside the index, model calls tagged by tenant for cost, and SSO with roles per project. Big customers can get an isolated deployment.
How does a deleted participant really disappear?
One delete workflow keyed by participant id: media in every region, transcripts, codes, embeddings, report caches and backups by expiry. Reports keep aggregate counts but drop the quotes.
wrap: Bottleneck: the analysis burst after a wave - queue per stage, batch small-model calls, scale workers on queue depth.
Risk: confident but unfounded insights - quote spans, verifiers, counts with ranges, and the clip one click away.
Cost: video storage and model calls dominate - transcode once, lifecycle old raw media, small models for coding.
Next: always-on studies (scheduled waves), API + MCP so customers' own agents can ask, more methods (pricing, MaxDiff).

Show stimuli (concept boards, videos, prototypes) at the right moment
Speak the question and show it on screen, in the participant's language
Pause, resume and finish on time
reqN: Participant stops speaking to next question: p95 under ~1.5 s
Same guide, same flow: researchers must trust the structure
Stay on topic; resist 'ignore your instructions' from participants
1,000s of sessions at once; a crashed worker loses nothing

~30 turns per 20-min interview; 1,000 live sessions ~ 25 turns/s - small model on every turn, big model rarely
Session state is tiny (guide position, probe count, last turns): a few KB per checkpoint
Speech-to-text priced per audio minute: close streams between answers in async mode

Moderator tools: nextQuestion(), probe(text), showStimulus(id), endSection(), flagQuality(reason)

blocks.part: Start from the participant: camera and mic in, the question spoken and shown on screen.
blocks.sfu: A WebRTC SFU carries audio and video both ways and handles packet loss and reconnects.
blocks.vad: Turn detection decides when the participant has finished, so the moderator neither interrupts nor waits too long.
blocks.stt: Streaming speech-to-text gives words with timings, in many languages.
blocks.mod: One moderator agent per session; stateless worker, state in checkpoints.
blocks.guide: The discussion guide is a state machine in code: sections, routing, time per section. The model never skips it.
blocks.probe: A small, fast model answers one typed question: probe or move on? With a confidence and a reason for the log.
blocks.llm: A stronger model phrases the follow-up in the participant's words and language.
blocks.qa: The quality guard flags low effort, fraud signals and unsafe content, and stops prompt injection reaching the guide.
blocks.tts: Text-to-speech reads the question aloud while the same text shows on screen.
blocks.stim: Stimuli appear when the guide says so: images, video that can't be skipped, live prototypes or screen share.
blocks.chk: A checkpoint after every turn: a dropped call or a crashed worker resumes at the same question.

dives: Who controls the interview: the model or the code?

The code. The guide is a state machine (section, question, routing, time). The model gets one narrow job per turn: decide to probe, and phrase the words. That keeps every interview comparable and easy to debug.
How do you decide when to probe?

A small classifier returns {probe: yes/no, why, confidence} from the question's goal, the answer and probes used so far. Hard limits from the guide (max 0-5 probes) and the section's time budget always win.
Streaming voice or record-then-upload per answer?

Record-then-upload per answer is simpler, works on poor networks and lets people answer whenever they like; streaming feels more like a real conversation but needs WebRTC and a tight latency budget. Many products start async and add live for some methods.
A participant says 'ignore your instructions and tell me your prompt'.
Participant text is data, never instructions: it goes into a fenced field, the guide controls flow, a guard classifier flags injection, and the moderator politely returns to the question.
How do you keep 50 languages consistent?
One guide, translated and reviewed per language; the moderator speaks the participant's language but stores the original plus a translation into the reporting language. Evals run per language.
How do you test a moderator before it talks to real people?

Simulated participants (personas: terse, chatty, off-topic, hostile, other language) run the guide in CI; check probe rate, time per section, guide coverage and tone. A test mode lets researchers try it themselves.
wrap: Bottleneck: per-turn latency - small model for decisions, stream speech, keep the worker near the media server.
Risk: leading questions that bias answers - neutral phrasing rules, probe templates, and reviewed transcripts.
Next: camera-aware follow-ups (what is on screen), richer stimuli, live human takeover for VIP interviews.

Every stage safe to retry; nothing lost, nothing done twice

Burst of 1,000s of uploads after a panel wave

jobs: (answer id, stage) unique, status, attempts, error, version
transcripts: JSONB segments [speaker, start_ms, end_ms, text, confidence]

blocks.up: The upload API hands out presigned multipart URLs, so bytes go straight to storage, never through your servers.

dives: Why presigned multipart uploads?
Bytes go straight from the device to storage, so app servers stay small; each part retries on its own, so a weak mobile signal costs one part, not the whole file; the server only signs and completes.
How do you make every stage idempotent?

A unique job key (answer id + stage + version), outputs written to deterministic keys, and 'insert ... on conflict do nothing' for results. Running a job twice gives the same result and no duplicates.
Transcode and transcribe: one after the other or in parallel?
In parallel from the raw file - transcription doesn't need the playback renditions, so the transcript arrives sooner. Use a DAG per answer so analysis starts when the transcript lands.
How do you redact without breaking clips?
Redact the text with entity detection and keep the timings; for media, bleep audio or blur only on export. Analysis reads the redacted transcript; raw stays locked down with short retention.
How would you build highlight reels?

Quotes store media start/end; a render job concatenates the segments with FFmpeg (or a managed media service), adds captions from the transcript, writes the result to storage and notifies the researcher.
wrap: Bottleneck: transcode capacity at peaks - autoscale workers on queue depth, or a managed media service.
Cost: storage dominates over time - lifecycle raw media to cold storage, keep only playback renditions.
Next: on-device compression, live captions, facial and tone signals as extra tracks.

Same input, same output: re-runs are stable
500 interviews analysed in under an hour

blocks.tr: Start from transcripts: segments with speakers and timestamps.
blocks.sp: Split each transcript into answers per question, so every unit of work is small and comparable.
blocks.code: The coder model returns typed output (code, quote span, sentiment) using a fixed schema - never free text.
blocks.cb: The codebook holds the study's codes with definitions and examples; the researcher can edit it.
blocks.vg: The quote verifier checks each span is really in the transcript and drops anything that isn't.
blocks.emb: An embedding model turns codes and quotes into vectors.
blocks.cl: Clustering groups similar codes into themes across interviews and keeps theme ids stable.

dives: How do you stop the model inventing quotes?
Ask for character offsets (or segment ids + offsets), not quote text. Verify the substring exists; drop or retry failures. The UI only ever shows text read back from the transcript.
How do you make re-runs stable?
Temperature 0, fixed model and prompt versions stored on every coding, a fixed codebook per run, and theme ids matched to the previous run by member overlap so names and links don't churn.
How do you turn 10k codes into 15 themes?

Embed codes, cluster (e.g. agglomerative or HDBSCAN), let a model name each cluster from its top quotes, then let the researcher merge and split. Keep a 'small themes' bucket instead of forcing everything in.
How do you know the coder is good?
A golden set coded by two researchers; measure agreement between humans first, then model vs humans per code. Ship only if precision and recall hold; track per language.
Counts for a segment of 12 people?
Show the count and a range (Wilson interval) and a note when the base is small; never present '58%' from 12 answers without its range.
wrap: Risk: themes that sound right but aren't supported - quotes first, counts with ranges, human review.
Cost: batch the coding calls (batch APIs, prompt caching of the codebook).
Next: track themes across waves of an always-on study, and alerts when a theme grows.

reqF: Ask a question in plain English across chosen studies, projects or all of them
Every claim in the answer cites quotes and clips
Count questions ('how many said...') use the coded data, not guesses
Always-on studies add new interviews every week
Customers' own AI assistants can query it through an API or MCP
reqN: Never show anything the asker can't see (tenant, project, study)
Answer in under ~10 s
Say when the evidence is thin instead of guessing
Answers show how fresh the evidence is
est: A big customer: 2,000 interviews/month x 12 months = 24k interviews ~ 500k answers to index
Index: themes (1,000s), quotes (100ks), transcript chunks (millions) - pgvector + text search per tenant fits for a long time
Per question: 3-5 sub-queries, top 100 -> rerank -> top 10 into the model ~ 5-8k tokens
api: MCP tools: search_quotes(query, filters), get_theme_counts(study, segment), list_studies()
data: index rows: tenant id, study id, type (theme | quote | chunk), text, embedding, date, segment tags
ACLs: user -> projects -> studies; checked inside the query
conversation threads with summaries of older turns

blocks.u: Start from the brand team: marketing, product and insights people asking questions in plain words.
blocks.ask: The ask agent plans sub-queries, picks counts vs quotes, and cites every claim.
blocks.perm: Permissions come from the session: tenant, project and study access. Never from the model.
blocks.hr: The hybrid retriever runs keyword and vector search together, with tenant and study filters inside the index.
blocks.idx: The index holds themes, quotes and transcript chunks with embeddings and text, tagged by tenant.
blocks.rr: A reranker picks the best 10 of the top 100.
blocks.llm: The model answers only from the evidence it is given, and says so when it is thin.
blocks.cit: Citations point to the quote and the clip, so anyone can check.
blocks.ing: Ingest adds new themes, quotes and transcripts as each study finishes.
blocks.wf: Always-on studies run waves on a schedule (weekly, monthly), so the base stays fresh.
blocks.mcp: An API and MCP server let customers' own agents ask the same agent, with the same permissions.

dives: How do you enforce permissions in RAG?

Filter inside the search (tenant id and allowed study ids in the WHERE clause or index filter), never after; identity comes from the session, not from anything the model writes; re-check before showing a citation.
'How many people mentioned price?' - RAG or SQL?
SQL over the coded data: themes and codes are already counted per segment. Retrieval is for 'why' and quotes. The agent picks the tool by question type.
How do you avoid confident answers on thin evidence?
Set a minimum number of supporting quotes, show the base size, and let the model answer 'not enough evidence in these studies' - test that case in evals.
How do you compare waves of an always-on study?
Keep the codebook stable across waves, count themes per wave, and show changes only when they are outside the range expected from sample size.
What changes when customers' agents call you over MCP?
Same agent and permissions, scoped tokens per customer, rate limits and usage metering, read-only tools, and answers that carry citations so their agent can show them.
wrap: Risk: leaking another study's quotes - filters in the query, tests that try to cross tenants.
Next: proactive digests ('what changed this week'), and agents that turn findings into actions.

reqF: Scroll an endless feed of posts (text and images), newest or ranked first
React to a post (like) and see it change instantly
Write a post (text and photo) that shows up in the feed at once
See a 'N new posts' pill when fresh posts arrive, never a sudden jump
Open a post and come back to the same scroll spot
reqN: Core Web Vitals 'good' at the 75th percentile: LCP 2.5 s or less, INP 200 ms or less, CLS 0.1 or less
Smooth on mid-range phones and slow 4G, so ship little JavaScript and keep the DOM small
Accessible (WCAG 2.2 AA): feed and article roles, keyboard reachable, focus never stolen
International: right-to-left text, plural rules, number and date formats
Safe: user text is never injected as HTML (XSS), strict Content Security Policy
est: Assume 20 posts per page and 3-4 posts above the fold on a phone, so the first response only needs page 1
Assume a first-load JavaScript budget of about 100-150 KB gzipped for the shell and about 300 KB for full interactivity (a common interview budget)
LCP time guide from web.dev: about 40% waiting for the server, about 40% loading the LCP resource, under 10% each for the two delays
Assume only ~10-20 posts are mounted in the DOM at any time, however far the user scrolled (virtualization)
Start the next fetch about one viewport before the end (IntersectionObserver rootMargin), so the user rarely sees a spinner
Count a post as seen after 50% visible for 1 second (a common impression rule), batch those events
api: GET /feed/stream (Server-Sent Events) -> event: new-posts, data: {count, newerCursor}
<Feed pages renderPost onNearEnd /> and <Post id onReact /> and <Composer onSubmit />
data: Server state (TanStack Query style): infinite query key ['feed', userId, 'home'], pages keyed by cursor, maxPages to cap memory
Normalized entities: postsById, usersById, mediaById - the feed is just an ordered list of post ids plus cursors, so one like updates every copy
Client state: composer draft, pending posts keyed by clientId, newPostsCount, scroll anchor (post id + pixel offset)
URL: /post/:id for detail; session storage for scroll restore; optional IndexedDB copy of page 1 for instant repeat visits
Never store user text as HTML - store plain text plus entity ranges (mentions, links)

blocks.u: A person on a phone or laptop scrolling, tapping like and writing posts.
blocks.shell: Server renders and streams the first page of posts as HTML so the largest element paints early, then the page hydrates.
blocks.feed: Renders only the posts near the viewport (virtualization) so the DOM stays small however far you scroll.
blocks.sent: An IntersectionObserver sentinel near the end of the list asks for the next page about one screen early.
blocks.qc: Caches each page by cursor, de-duplicates in-flight requests and allows only one next-page fetch at a time.
blocks.api: Cursor-paginated GET /feed returns post ids plus the posts and users they need.
blocks.norm: Keeps posts and users by id so every copy of a post on screen updates together.
blocks.comp: Adds your new post to the top at once with a temporary id, then swaps in the server post or rolls back on error.
blocks.live: A Server-Sent Events stream only says 'N new posts exist'; the pill lets the user choose when to load them.
blocks.img: Responsive images with srcset, AVIF or WebP, reserved width and height, lazy below the fold and high priority for the LCP image.
blocks.cdn: Serves resized, cached images close to the user.
blocks.rum: Real-user monitoring reports LCP, INP and CLS by device and network so regressions show up in the field.

dives: Why cursor pagination instead of page numbers?

New posts arrive at the top, so offset pages shift and show duplicates or gaps. An opaque cursor points at a stable position and can be tied to a feed generation so a re-ranked feed asks for a refresh.
Infinite scroll makes the DOM huge. What do you do?

Virtualize (windowing): mount only the posts near the viewport plus a small overscan, with spacers for the rest. Keep the focused post mounted and restore scroll by anchoring to a post id and offset, because heights are variable.
The sentinel fires twice and you load the same page twice. How do you prevent it?

Allow a single in-flight next-page fetch (check isFetching, TanStack Query allows only one ongoing fetch per infinite query), key pages by cursor, and re-observe the sentinel after each load so it fires again if it is still visible.
How do likes and new posts feel instant yet stay correct?

Optimistic update: change the entity at once, send the request with an idempotency key, and roll back on failure (React useOptimistic reverts automatically when the real state does not change). Because entities are normalized, every copy updates together.
New posts arrive while the user reads. What is the UX and the transport?

Show a 'N new posts' pill and prepend only on click, so the content under the finger never jumps. Server-Sent Events are enough because traffic is one-way, the browser reconnects by itself and resumes with Last-Event-ID; use HTTP/2 because HTTP/1.1 allows only about 6 connections per domain.
SSR or client-side rendering for the signed-in feed?

A personal feed is highly interactive and long-lived, so client rendering with a tight JS budget is a valid default, while public permalinks and logged-out pages benefit from SSR. Here we stream the first page from the server for LCP and hydrate only the interactive parts.
How do you make it accessible?

Use role='feed' with role='article' per post, aria-busy while a page loads, keyboard-reachable actions, polite live region for the new-posts pill, 24x24 CSS px minimum targets (WCAG 2.2) and respect prefers-reduced-motion. Never move focus when new data arrives.
Security and i18n in post content?

Render text from plain text plus entity ranges, never innerHTML, validate link schemes and ship a Content Security Policy. Use dir='auto' on post bodies, CSS logical properties for RTL and Intl.NumberFormat / Intl.PluralRules for counts like '103K'.
wrap: Bottleneck: the first page decides LCP and a long session grows the DOM and memory. Fix: stream page 1 with a priority image, virtualize, cap cached pages (maxPages).
Next: ranked feed, comments thread, offline outbox for posts, experiments with feature flags and a field-data dashboard.

Highlight the part of each suggestion that matches the query
Reusable: the host app supplies the data fetcher and how an item looks
Clear states for loading, no results, error and offline

Always correct: a slow older reply can never overwrite a newer query
Accessible: follows the WAI-ARIA combobox pattern with a live region
Works on mobile and with IME input (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) and RTL
Small and framework friendly, no XSS from suggestion text
est: Debounce about 300 ms (a common default) so a fast typist sends one request, not one per key
Start at 1-3 characters (a common minimum is 3 for large corpora); make it a prop
Assume 5-10 suggestions per response and about 1 KB of JSON per response
Assume a cache of ~100 queries with a TTL and least-recently-used eviction, so memory stays tiny
INP target 200 ms or less at p75: render the list in one commit per response
WCAG 2.2 minimum target size is 24x24 CSS px for each suggestion row
api: fetcher(query, {limit, signal: AbortSignal}) -> Promise<Item[]>   (the only place that knows URLs and auth)
<Autocomplete fetcher minChars={2} debounceMs={300} limit={8} cacheTtlMs={60000} onSelect renderItem />

Results cache: Map<normalizedQuery, {items, fetchedAt}> with TTL and LRU cap; normalize by trim, lowercase and Unicode NFC

No URL state until the user submits a search

blocks.u: A person typing, using arrows, Enter and Escape, maybe with an IME or a screen reader.
blocks.in: The text box with role=combobox; focus stays here while aria-activedescendant points at the highlighted option.
blocks.deb: Waits until typing pauses (about 300 ms) before asking for suggestions.
blocks.cache: Remembers results per normalized query with a TTL and LRU cap, so backspacing or retyping costs nothing.
blocks.api: Sends the request with an AbortSignal and a generation number so only the newest reply is accepted.
blocks.srv: The suggest endpoint returns a short ranked list of items with stable ids.
blocks.st: Holds query, results, status and the active index as the single source of truth for the UI.
blocks.list: Renders the listbox, highlights the matched text safely and handles pointer and key selection.
blocks.live: A polite live region announces things like '5 results' or 'No results' to screen readers.

dives: A slow reply for 'ca' arrives after the reply for 'cat'. How do you stop the wrong list showing?

Give every request a generation number and only render a reply whose query matches the current input and whose generation is the newest. AbortController cancels wasted work but is not the correctness mechanism, since an aborted request can still race.
Debounce, throttle or useDeferredValue?

Debounce for network calls (wait for a pause). Throttle suits continuous signals like scroll. React's useDeferredValue keeps typing responsive while the list renders but does not stop requests, so combine it with debouncing.
What does the accessible pattern look like?

Follow the WAI-ARIA combobox: input role=combobox with aria-expanded and aria-controls, popup role=listbox, options role=option, DOM focus stays on the input and aria-activedescendant tracks the highlighted row. Down Arrow opens or moves, Enter accepts, Escape closes, plus an aria-live region for counts.
Why can Enter select the wrong thing with Chinese or Japanese input?
During IME composition the keys belong to the input method. Ignore navigation keys while composing and only search on the committed value after compositionend.
How do you highlight the match without XSS?
Split the suggestion text into matched and unmatched parts and render them as text nodes or <mark> elements. Never build the string with innerHTML from server data.
Clicking a suggestion closes the popup before the click lands. Why?
Blur fires before click. Prevent default on pointer down in the list or delay closing on blur until pointer activation is handled, otherwise the row is unmounted mid-click.
How do you design the cache?

A query to results map is enough for a short-lived widget. Key by the normalized full query, add a TTL and an LRU cap, and clear it when the user signs out. A client-side trie only helps for a small, stable local list, because server results may be top-k only.
Errors and offline?
Show a retry for server errors, back off if the server is overloaded, and when offline serve only cached results and show a small no-connection state. Keep the typed text so nothing is lost.
wrap: Bottleneck: races and per-keystroke work, not the server. Fix: debounce, generation guard, cache, one commit per reply.
Next: fuzzy matching, recent and trending sections, rich result types (images), analytics on selection rank.

reqF: Send and receive text messages in 1:1 and group threads in real time
A sent message appears at once and shows its state: sending, sent, delivered, read
Thread list with last message, unread badge and newest first
Scroll up to load older history; open a thread at the newest message
Offline: keep typing, messages wait in an outbox and send when back online
A notification when the tab is closed; several open tabs stay in sync
reqN: No lost, duplicated or out-of-order messages, even across reconnects
Typing stays smooth (INP 200 ms or less at p75) in threads with thousands of messages
Resilient: reconnect with backoff and jitter, then catch up on what was missed
Accessible: new messages announced politely, keyboard-first composer, WCAG 2.2 AA
International: emoji, IME input, right-to-left text; safe: text escaped, auth on the socket handshake
est: Assume 50 messages loaded when a thread opens and 50 more per scroll-up page
Assume only ~30-60 message rows are mounted in the DOM (virtualized), however long the thread
Assume ONE WebSocket per browser (leader tab), not one per tab

Browsers do not reconnect a WebSocket or send heartbeats for you: assume an app ping about every 30 s and reconnect backoff 1 s doubling to a 30 s cap, plus random jitter so a server restart does not cause a thundering herd (a common pattern, not built into the API)
Assume IndexedDB keeps the last ~20 threads x 50 messages for instant open and offline reading
Server-Sent Events over HTTP/1.1 are limited to about 6 connections per domain across tabs, which is one reason to prefer one shared WebSocket
api: WS client -> server: {type:'send', threadId, clientId, text}
WS server -> client: {type:'ack', clientId, id, seq, ts}  and  {type:'message', threadId, id, seq, from, text, ts}
WS: {type:'receipt', threadId, upToSeq, kind:'delivered'|'read'}, {type:'typing', threadId} (throttled), {type:'sync', threadId, afterSeq} -> missed messages
data: Normalized store: messagesById, threadMessageIds[threadId] ordered by server seq, threadsById, lastSeq per thread, unreadCount
Pending messages keyed by clientId with status (queued | sending | sent | failed); on ack swap to the server id and drop the temp entry
Outbox persisted in IndexedDB so a refresh or crash loses nothing
Recent threads and messages cached in IndexedDB; draft text per thread in localStorage or IndexedDB
Cross-tab: BroadcastChannel for events, Web Locks to elect the one tab that owns the socket
URL: /t/:threadId so a thread is linkable and back works

blocks.u: A person writing and reading messages, sometimes offline, sometimes in several tabs.
blocks.ui: Thread list, message pane and composer; the composer never blocks while the network is slow.
blocks.out: Queues each message with a temporary clientId, shows it at once and retries until the server acknowledges it.
blocks.ws: Owns the WebSocket: heartbeat, reconnect with backoff and jitter, and a catch-up request after the last known seq.
blocks.gw: Server side of the socket: authenticates the handshake, assigns the per-thread sequence and fans messages out.
blocks.store: Keeps messages normalized and ordered by server sequence, merges acks and receipts, and de-duplicates by id and clientId.
blocks.vl: Renders only nearby messages, anchored to the bottom, and keeps the scroll position stable when history loads.
blocks.idb: Persists recent threads, messages and the outbox so the app opens instantly and survives refreshes and offline.
blocks.bc: Shares updates between tabs with Broadcast Channel so unread counts and drafts stay consistent.
blocks.push: Web Push delivers a notification when no tab is open.
blocks.sw: The service worker receives the push event and shows the notification, then focuses or opens the right thread on click.

dives: How do you avoid duplicates and show a message at once?

Create a clientId on send and render the message immediately as pending. The server echoes it in an ack with the real id and seq, and the store replaces the pending entry. On retry the same clientId makes the send idempotent.
How do you order messages?
By the server-assigned sequence per thread, not by device clocks or arrival order. Pending messages sit at the bottom until acked, then take their seq position.
The connection drops for 30 seconds. What happens on reconnect?
Reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, re-authenticate, then send a sync request with the last seq per open thread and merge the missed messages. Resend the outbox with the same clientIds.
WebSocket, Server-Sent Events or polling?

Chat needs two-way, low-latency traffic, so WebSocket. SSE is one-way (and HTTP/1.1 limits it to about 6 connections per domain), polling wastes battery. WebSocket has no built-in reconnect, heartbeat or backpressure, so the client adds the first two.
How does the message list stay smooth and not jump?

Virtualize with a bottom-anchored list: auto-scroll on new messages only if the user is already near the bottom, show a 'new messages' button otherwise, and preserve the scroll anchor when older pages are prepended.
Three tabs are open. How many sockets?
One. Elect a leader with a Web Lock (navigator.locks.request with ifAvailable) and relay messages to other tabs over BroadcastChannel; if the leader closes, the lock frees and another tab takes over.
How do offline sends work?
Persist the outbox in IndexedDB and flush when the socket is back. Background Sync can help but has limited browser availability, so keep an in-page retry as the primary path.
Notifications when the tab is closed?

Register a service worker, ask for permission after a user action, subscribe with PushManager (userVisibleOnly: true) and send the subscription to the server. The worker's push event must show a notification, and the click should open the thread.
wrap: Bottleneck: correctness around reconnects and many tabs, then rendering long threads. Fix: client ids and server seq, sync-after-seq, one leader socket, virtualized list.
Next: group presence at scale, attachments with upload progress, end-to-end encryption, search over local history.

Endless scroll that loads the next batch before the user hits the bottom

Related images below the detail view

Assume ~50-100 image nodes mounted at once (virtualized window plus overscan), not thousands
Blur placeholder is a tiny string or inline image sent in the API response (assume tens of bytes to a few hundred bytes)

GET /pins/:id -> {pin, author, stats}  and  GET /pins/:id/related?cursor= -> {items, nextCursor}
Image URL on the CDN: /img/:id?w=474&fmt=avif (width and format as parameters, edge resizes and caches)
<Masonry items columnWidth gutter renderItem virtualize overscan onLoadMore />

Viewport state: scrollTop, containerWidth (debounced resize) decide the visible slice

Nothing in IndexedDB at first; placeholder (blurhash or color) comes with each item

blocks.u: A person scrolling a grid of images, hovering and opening details.
blocks.ssr: Server renders the first grid with real dimensions and a priority image so the first screen paints fast.
blocks.grid: Places each item in the currently shortest column using its width and height ratio, so positions are known before any image loads.
blocks.vw: Mounts only the items near the viewport and keeps the rest as empty positioned space.
blocks.inf: Loads the next cursor page when a sentinel gets close to the viewport.
blocks.qc: Caches pages by cursor and avoids duplicate requests while scrolling fast.
blocks.api: Returns each pin with width, height, alt text and a tiny blur placeholder.
blocks.img: Uses srcset and sizes, AVIF or WebP, width and height set, lazy loading below the fold and a blur placeholder.
blocks.cdn: Resizes and caches images at the edge so each device downloads only the size it needs.
blocks.modal: Opens the detail as a URL-driven overlay and prefetches the pin on hover or focus.

dives: How do you place items in a masonry layout?

Know each item's height before it loads: height = columnWidth x (h / w) from the API, plus any fixed caption. Place the next item in the shortest column and record its top and column. Positions never change when later pages append.
Why must the API send width and height?

The browser needs space reserved before the file arrives. Setting width and height on the img (or CSS aspect-ratio) lets it compute the ratio, which prevents layout shift and lets the layout engine position items without waiting.
How do you virtualize a masonry grid?

Because positions are absolute and known, render only items whose box intersects the viewport plus an overscan margin, with the container height set to the tallest column. Recompute columns when the container width changes (debounced), not on every scroll.
What is your image loading strategy?

First row: eager with fetchpriority=high on one or two images; everything else loading=lazy. Use srcset with width descriptors and sizes, serve AVIF or WebP from the CDN, and show a blur placeholder until decode.
Keyboard and screen reader order in columns?

DOM order should be the placement order (by item index), not column by column, so tabbing follows what the user sees. Give every image meaningful alt text, and in the modal trap focus, close on Escape and return focus to the tile.
How does the detail modal work with URLs?

The route /pin/:id drives the overlay: opening from the grid pushes the URL and shows an overlay (intercepting route), while a direct visit renders the full page. Share, refresh and back all behave. Prefetch the pin on hover or focus.
Memory and jank on a phone?
Unmount off-screen tiles, use decoding=async, request right-sized images, avoid animating layout properties and keep a stable key per pin so React does not remount tiles when pages append.
Native CSS masonry instead of JavaScript?

Native masonry (display: grid-lanes in the draft spec) is still experimental in stable browsers, so use it only as progressive enhancement behind @supports. Note that placement can make tab order differ from visual order.
wrap: Bottleneck: layout shift and too many big images decoding at once. Fix: dimensions from the API, right-sized AVIF or WebP from an image CDN, virtualized window, lazy below the fold.
Next: drag to save, personalised related pins, offline cache of saved pins, field-data dashboard.

Experiments (A/B) and recommendations without slowing the page

Accessible forms and flows (WCAG 2.2 AA): labels, errors, keyboard, focus

<BuyBox sku variants onAdd /> <Gallery images /> <FilterPanel facets value onChange /> <CartDrawer />

blocks.cdn: Serves cached HTML and static assets from the edge so most pages never reach the origin.
blocks.isr: Product pages are prebuilt and refreshed in the background on a timer or when a price changes (stale-while-revalidate).
blocks.rsc: Server Components fetch catalog data on the server, send HTML and ship no JavaScript for static parts.
blocks.api: Catalog, price and cart services behind one gateway the server and the client call.
blocks.isl: Only the gallery, variant picker and buy box ship JavaScript and hydrate.
blocks.cart: Adds items instantly in the UI, sends the change to the server cart and reconciles with the server's answer.

dives: Which rendering mode for which page?

Home, category and product: static or ISR at the CDN for SEO and speed, with price and stock streamed in. Search results: server rendered from the URL. Cart and checkout: dynamic, no-store, personal. Choose per route instead of one mode for the whole site.
A price changes. How does the product page update?

Use on-demand revalidation (for example revalidateTag on the product) so the next request rebuilds the page, and keep the live price in a small streamed or client-fetched section so the cached shell is never wrong about money.
Where do filters live and what about SEO?

In the URL as query params so pages are shareable and back works. Give real <a href> links and a unique URL per page, and keep filtered or oddly sorted combinations out of the index (noindex or robots rules), while important category pages stay indexable.
How does the cart stay correct?

The server cart is the truth. The UI updates optimistically (useOptimistic), sends the change, then replaces local state with the server response; stock or price conflicts are shown clearly. Keep cartId in an httpOnly cookie and merge guest and account carts on sign-in.
How do you keep card data out of your app?

Use the payment provider's hosted fields (Stripe Elements-style iframes): card details go straight to the provider and never touch your servers, which keeps PCI scope small. Add the provider to your Content Security Policy and use HTTPS everywhere.
Third-party scripts and A/B tests hurt speed. What do you do?
Resolve flags on the server or edge so there is no flicker or layout shift, load tags after interaction or in a worker, set budgets, and watch INP and CLS per experiment variant.
How do you make checkout accessible and easy to finish?

Real labels, autocomplete attributes, inline errors tied with aria-describedby and moved focus to the first error, large tap targets (24x24 CSS px minimum), and support wallets or express checkout to skip typing.
Traffic spike on a sale day. What protects the site?

Cache pages at the CDN with stale-while-revalidate, keep personal parts as small streamed islands with Suspense and error boundaries, degrade recommendations first and make orders idempotent so retries are safe.

dives: How does adaptive bitrate (ABR) choose a quality?

It measures recent segment download speed and watches buffer level. hls.js only steps up when 0.7 x bandwidth beats the next bitrate, and steps down when 0.95 x bandwidth falls below the current one, so it climbs slowly and drops quickly to avoid stalls.
How do you make the first frame appear fast?

Preconnect to the CDN and fetch the manifest early (even before the user clicks), start on a low or middle rendition, show a poster image instantly, and keep the player script small and deferred. hls.js can also prefetch the first fragment with startFragPrefetch.
What does MSE actually do?

MSE replaces a single src URL with a MediaSource and SourceBuffer. Your code downloads segments and calls appendBuffer after each updateend, and the browser decodes them. This is why quality can change mid-stream: you just append a segment from a different rendition.
How does DRM fit in?

EME: ask requestMediaKeySystemAccess for Widevine, PlayReady or FairPlay, create MediaKeys, and on the encrypted event create a session, send its challenge to your licence server and pass the licence back. Needs HTTPS. Keys stay inside the CDM.
Accessibility of a custom player?

Use real buttons with names, a slider role for seek with aria-valuetext as a time, visible focus, WebVTT captions on by preference, no autoplay with sound, and respect prefers-reduced-motion for hover animations.
How do you avoid wasting data and memory?

Cap quality to the player size (hls.js capLevelToPlayerSize), keep the forward buffer bounded, evict the back buffer, and pause loading when the tab is hidden. ManagedMediaSource lets Safari evict buffer under memory pressure.
How do you handle errors and stalls?
Retry a segment with backoff, then step down a rendition, then try another CDN host from the manifest. Fatal errors show a plain message with a retry button; every error is sent to QoE with its type.
How do you test it?
Throttle the network in devtools to rehearse low bandwidth, run a matrix of browsers and devices, use a fixture stream with known renditions, and watch real-user QoE dashboards after release.
wrap: Bottleneck: startup time and rebuffering on poor networks. Fix: early manifest fetch, low first rendition, cautious ABR and CDN failover.
Next: low-latency live, offline downloads with persistent licences, Picture-in-Picture and casting.

dives: CRDT or OT (operational transform)?

OT needs a central server to order and transform operations; ProseMirror's own collab module works that way with a single authority that rejects and rebases. A CRDT like Yjs merges updates in any order, which makes offline and peer-to-peer natural, at the cost of metadata growth that Yjs compacts well.
Why apply edits locally first?
Waiting for a server round trip on every key would feel laggy. The editor applies the transaction at once (optimistic), the CRDT encodes it as an update, and the network catches up in the background.
How do cursors and comments stay correct while text changes?
Never store numeric offsets. Use Yjs relative positions, which point at an item in the CRDT, so they follow the text when others insert or delete before it.
How is presence different from document data?
Awareness is ephemeral: small JSON per user, overwritten by a newer clock, timed out after 30 s of silence, throttled when the cursor moves, and never stored. Losing a message is fine.
What does undo mean with many people?
Undo only your own changes. Y.UndoManager tracks the local origin so it will not revert a collaborator's paragraph.
Performance in long documents?

Keep the editor schema simple, avoid re-rendering the whole tree (decorations for cursors), debounce toolbar state, offload heavy work to a worker and consider splitting very large docs into sub-documents.
Accessibility?

Use contenteditable with proper roles and labels, keep native selection, announce collaborator joins politely (aria-live), make every toolbar action keyboard reachable and keep colour-only cursors readable with name labels.
Security of pasted and shared content?
Parse paste through the editor schema so only allowed nodes survive, sanitise URLs, check permissions on the server for every connection, and never trust awareness data as HTML.
wrap: Bottleneck: large documents and long histories growing the CRDT. Fix: sub-documents, lazy sections, periodic snapshots and garbage collection.
